title: How to Organize a Spice Drawer: A Step-by-Step System You Can Keep
excerpt: How to organize a spice drawer step by step: measure, edit, choose jars and inserts, label tops, sort by how you cook, and keep the system tidy with a simple routine.
content: To **organize a spice drawer**, empty and measure it, keep only the seasonings you use, choose jars and an insert that fit, label the visible surface, and sort jars by how you cook. Put everyday spices at the front and give refills a separate labeled home. Choose a cool, dry drawer away from cooktop heat, not simply the closest space to the pan. This step-by-step guide shows how to create a layout you can maintain without buying a matching set of everything.

We cover choosing the right drawer, measuring it, editing your collection, picking jars and inserts, labeling, sorting by how you cook and keeping the drawer under control. If your kitchen has no spare drawer, we also include cabinet alternatives that give you the same at-a-glance view. For broader kitchen planning, our [kitchen drawer organizer ideas](/blog/kitchen-drawer-organizer-ideas-transform-cooking-space-2026) and [spice rack organization](/blog/spice-rack-organization) guides are good companions.
## Why a Drawer Beats a Cabinet for Spices

In a cabinet, jars sit in rows, and you can only read the front row. Tiered risers help, but the back still disappears. In a drawer, every jar faces up, so the whole collection is visible in a single glance. That visibility saves time while cooking and money at the store, because you stop buying a third jar of paprika.
A drawer near the stove also keeps spices where you use them. You can open it with one hand while stirring with the other, which is not true of a high cabinet that requires reaching over a hot pan.
The trade-off is that drawers are shallow and jars must lie down or stand on short inserts. That makes jar choice and labeling more important than in a cabinet. The steps below handle both.
## Step 1: Choose and Measure the Drawer

Choose a drawer near your prep area only if it stays cool and dry. Avoid one directly under a warm cooktop or beside a source of steam. [University of Delaware Cooperative Extension's spice-storage guidance](https://www.udel.edu/academics/colleges/canr/cooperative-extension/fact-sheets/using-herbs-and-spices/) recommends airtight containers away from heat and direct sunlight. Convenience should not put the jars in a hot storage zone.
Measure three things before you buy anything:
1. **Interior width,** from side to side, inside the drawer box.
2. **Interior depth,** from front to back, minus any space the drawer slides need.
3. **Usable height,** from the drawer floor to the underside of the countertop or the drawer above when it closes.
Write the numbers down and take them shopping. Height is the one people forget, and it decides whether jars can stand upright or must lie on an angled insert.

![Diagram of a spice drawer seen from above, divided into rows for everyday spices at the front, baking spices and blends in the middle, and refills at the back, with notes on measuring width, depth and height](/images/blog/how-to-organize-spice-drawer-layout-diagram.svg)
## Step 2: Empty, Check and Edit Your Spices
Take every spice out of every cabinet, drawer and pantry shelf and put them on the counter together. This is the only way to see duplicates and forgotten jars.

Check each jar for quality. [N.C. Cooperative Extension explains](https://rutherford.ces.ncsu.edu/news/cooking-with-herbs-spice/) that light, heat and moisture shorten the useful flavor life of dried herbs and spices, and that aroma can help you judge their potency. Smell a small amount to decide whether it will contribute enough flavor to your cooking. This is a flavor check, not a guarantee that a product is free of contamination; follow package instructions and do not keep visibly spoiled or damaged products.

Combine duplicates into one container where the spices are the same. Set aside anything you bought for a single recipe and never used again. If you are not sure whether you will use it, put it in a small "maybe" box and revisit it in a few months.
The goal is a collection that reflects how you actually cook. Many households use a core set of spices weekly and the rest rarely. Knowing which is which shapes the layout in Step 5.
## Step 3: Choose Jars That Fit the Drawer
Matching jars make a spice drawer far easier to scan, because the eye reads labels instead of a mix of shapes and colors. They also pack more tightly than mismatched store containers.

| Jar style | Best for | Things to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Small round glass jars | Most ground spices and herbs | Lid label space, fit on an angled insert |
| Square glass jars | Maximizing space in a row | Corners waste less room than round jars |
| Flat tins with clear lids | Shallow drawers, lying flat | Label the lid; check the seal |
| Original store jars | Keeping costs low | Mixed heights make inserts harder to use |
| Larger jars | Salt, pepper, everyday blends | Keep them at the front where you reach most |

Choose jars with lids that close securely and openings you can clean and dry fully. [Delaware Extension recommends tightly closed storage](https://www.udel.edu/academics/colleges/canr/cooperative-extension/fact-sheets/using-herbs-and-spices/), including glass jars, suitable plastic bags or stainless steel containers for dried herbs. The container material does not remove the need to protect spices from heat, light and moisture. For the broader trade-offs when choosing kitchen containers, read our [glass, plastic and steel comparison](/blog/glass-vs-plastic-vs-stainless-steel-food-storage-containers).

If you decant spices from bags or bulk bins, use a small funnel and fill jars over a tray so spills are easy to tip back in. Write the purchase month on a small sticker under the lid so you know how old each refill is.
## Step 4: Pick the Right Insert
Inserts keep jars in rows so they do not roll every time the drawer opens. There are three main types:
1. **Angled tiered inserts** hold jars at a slant, so labels on the lid or the side face you. They suit drawers with moderate height.
2. **Flat grid or slotted inserts** hold jars lying down, label side up, which works in shallow drawers.
3. **Expandable inserts** adjust to the drawer width, which is handy if your drawer is an odd size.

Non-slip drawer liner under the insert stops the whole thing from sliding. If you prefer not to buy an insert at all, rows of small rectangular containers or even a rolled kitchen towel between rows can keep jars from rolling, though they look less tidy.
If your kitchen has no free drawer near the stove, you can create one. A slide-out drawer mounted inside a base cabinet gives you the same top-down view.

## Step 5: Label Smart and Sort by How You Cook

Label every jar on the lid if the jars lie flat or stand upright, because the lid is what you see from above. If you use an angled insert, label the side that faces you. Use the same font, size and position on every jar. Printed labels are easiest to read, but neat handwriting on round stickers works just as well.
Then decide on an order. Three common systems:
1. **Alphabetical:** simple and easy for everyone in the house to follow. Best for large collections.
2. **By frequency:** everyday spices at the front, occasional ones at the back. Fastest for daily cooking.
3. **By cuisine or use:** baking spices together, chili and cumin together, Italian herbs together. Great if you cook a few styles often.

Many cooks combine them: frequency decides which zone a spice goes in, and alphabetical order applies within each zone. Salt, pepper and your two or three most used spices sit closest to the front of the drawer.

## Step 6: Handle Refills, Blends and Packets

Bulk bags and spice packets are where drawer systems usually break down. Give refills their own home instead of letting them float around. A small lidded box at the back of the spice drawer, or a labeled bin in the pantry, works well. Fold bags tightly and clip them, or decant them into a larger jar.

Seasoning packets for tacos, chili or gravy can stand on edge in a narrow container like files in a cabinet, so you can flip through them. Homemade blends deserve a jar and a label with the date you made them.

Keep a short list on the inside of a cabinet door or on your phone of spices that are running low. When you use the last of a jar, add it to the list right away, and your next shopping trip will cover it.

## Keep the Spice Drawer Organized

A spice drawer stays organized when putting a jar back is easier than leaving it out. Return each jar to its labeled spot right after use. Wipe spills promptly, since spilled turmeric or paprika can stain a drawer liner.

Every few months, do a quick check: smell a few jars from the back, merge any new duplicates and move spices you have started using more often toward the front. Wash and dry empty jars before refilling, and make sure they are completely dry, because moisture causes clumping.

If the drawer starts overflowing, that is a sign to edit rather than to buy a bigger insert. Our guide on [how to keep your kitchen organized](/blog/how-to-keep-your-kitchen-organized) covers daily habits that support every zone of the kitchen, not just spices.

## Frequently Asked Questions About How to Organize a Spice Drawer
**Q: What is the best way to organize a spice drawer?**
Empty and edit your spices, move them into matching jars, use an angled or slotted insert so jars stay in rows, label the lids, and place the spices you use most at the front of the drawer.
**Q: Should spice jars lie down or stand up in a drawer?**
It depends on drawer height. In shallow drawers, lay jars down with labels on top or use an angled insert. In deeper drawers, jars can stand upright with labels on the lids.
**Q: Where should a spice drawer be in the kitchen?**
Close to the stove or main prep area, ideally a top drawer, but not directly under the cooktop if that drawer gets warm, since heat makes spices lose flavor faster.
**Q: Should I organize spices alphabetically?**
Alphabetical order is easy for everyone to follow and works well for large collections. Many cooks keep their most used spices at the front and sort the rest alphabetically.
**Q: How do I know if a spice is too old to use?**

Check its aroma and color to assess flavor strength, as described by [N.C. Cooperative Extension](https://rutherford.ces.ncsu.edu/news/cooking-with-herbs-spice/). Replace a spice that no longer contributes useful flavor. Smell is not a food-safety test, so follow the package instructions and discard visibly spoiled or damaged products rather than relying on aroma alone.
**Q: What do I do with spice refills and bulk bags?**
Give them a dedicated home, such as a lidded box at the back of the drawer or a labeled pantry bin. Decant into larger jars or fold and clip the bags tightly.
**Q: Can I organize spices without matching jars?**
Yes. Group store jars by height, label the lids, and use a tiered insert so taller jars sit at the back. Matching jars simply make the drawer easier to scan.
**Q: How do I make a spice drawer if my kitchen has none to spare?**
Add a slide-out drawer inside a base cabinet, or use a pull-out or swivel spice rack in a cabinet so the back row comes forward when you need it.
## Conclusion: A Spice Drawer That Saves Time Every Day

Learning how to organize a spice drawer comes down to six steps: pick the right drawer and measure it, edit your collection, choose jars that fit, add an insert, label and sort by how you cook, and give refills their own home. With every lid visible and every spice in a predictable spot, cooking gets faster and duplicate purchases stop.
